Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette:
Daniel Rangi, a 39-year-old divorced airline pilot of Oceanian background, came to treatment after months of feeling as if his body and mind had never fully left a single police encounter that had turned violent and chaotic. He had been stopped late at night after a minor traffic issue, and what began as a routine exchange escalated when multiple officers crowded close, shouted over one another, and reached for him while he was still seated in the car. He remembers the press of bodies near the door, the confined space, the smell of the vehicle closing in around him, and the nauseating surge that hit him as he realized he could not easily move away. Even now, when he thinks back on it, the scene comes back with the same terror he felt in that moment; he says it is not like recalling an ordinary event, but like being dropped back into it, with the memory feeling more real and vivid than his day-to-day life, yet also so extreme that it hardly seems believable it happened to him at all.

In the weeks after that night, Daniel began to react to situations that once would have seemed unremarkable. Being physically close to other people, especially when someone approached him in a corridor or stood too near in a queue, could make his chest tighten and his stomach turn. Riding in a car with other people became difficult, not because of driving itself, but because sitting beside someone in a confined space brought back the sense of being trapped and exposed. The nausea was especially striking to him; if it appeared, he would immediately think of the stop, the officers, and the helplessness of being surrounded, and his body would seem to prepare for danger before he had consciously identified why. Those moments of bodily alarm made the present feel contaminated by the past, and the more often they happened, the more Daniel came to expect that something bad might be about to unfold whenever he felt crowded, motioned toward by a stranger, or physically unable to create distance.

That expectation spread into a broader sense of threat. If an elevator took too long to arrive, if a colleague was delayed in meeting him, or if a routine process at work ran behind schedule, he would assume that something bad was happening somewhere he could not see. Ordinary sounds at home or in the airport terminal-an abrupt bang, a dropped suitcase, someone calling out sharply-made him jump in a way that embarrassed him, but which he could not stop. He also found himself watching strangers with particular vigilance, certain that someone approaching in an ordinary setting could become threatening without warning. Because he felt so alert to danger, Daniel started noticing the very conditions that reminded him of the original encounter: people moving too close, being stuck in a vehicle with others, the uneasy churn in his stomach, or any delay that left him unable to reassure himself that everything was under control. Those moments of monitoring brought the whole event back into sharper focus. He would think of the police stop, and the memory's vividness would intensify again, making it feel even more immediate and more real.

As the months passed, Daniel's world narrowed around this pattern. He began arranging his days to avoid situations that produced proximity or the possibility of driving with others, and he found himself creating distance at work whenever he could, even though his occupation as an airline pilot made him spend long stretches in controlled, confined environments that he had once navigated with ease. He became wary of preflight delays and ground interruptions, not simply because they were inconvenient but because any slowdown now felt loaded with threat, as if delay itself signaled that something dangerous was building just out of sight. In the airport, he would scan the crowd for strangers who seemed to be coming too close, and in the car on the way home he would sit rigidly, listening for sounds that might make him startle. The more he organized his life around avoiding these moments, the more he felt the original terror lingering beneath the surface, ready to return. Daniel was divorced, and he noticed that his avoidance and vigilance had begun to spill into his relationships as well; plans were harder to make, conversations became shorter, and he found himself explaining less and withdrawing more, because he did not trust his own reactions in close quarters.

By the time he sought help, Daniel described feeling trapped in a loop that began with the memory and then reshaped the present. Remembering the arrest brought back the same terror, and that terror made ordinary closeness, delays, strangers, and shared rides feel dangerous; those experiences, in turn, made the memory come alive again with unbearable force. He had finally come to treatment because the cycle was interfering with his work and making him feel less and less safe in situations that other people appeared to move through without thought. What he most feared was that he would keep living as though the night of the police stop were still happening, and what he most hoped for was to be able to sit near other people, ride in a car, and hear an ordinary sound without his body convincing him that danger was already there.
